newsitem.title: USA: U.S. ag industry represented in force at WTO meeting.
newsitem.headline: U.S. ag industry represented in force at WTO meeting.

text.p: The U.S. agriculture industry is slated to have a big presence at next week's World Trade Organisation ministerial meeting in Singapore, with more than a third of the sizeable U.S. delegation comprised of "aggies."

Interested in issues ranging from China's possible entry into the WTO to Europe's current worries over new U.S. gene-altered crops, American agriculture will be represented by at least 55 officials from the administration, Congress, trade and producer groups and private food companies.

At last count, the entire U.S. delegation totalled 148. The group will be led by Acting U.S. Trade Representive Charlene Barshefsky. The ranking official for agricultural issues will be Deputy Agriculture Secretary Richard Rominger.
"We want to demonstrate how important agriculture is to the United States and impress that to the world," said Rominger. "There is a lot of work to do to continue to reduce the (trade) barriers."
"I think it's really important that we're there and showing a unified presence," said Ken Hobbie, president of the U.S. Feed Grains Council, shortly before he left for Asia.

While Hobbie and others said they were not looking for any new agreements to be solidified at the conference, they said that just having access to policy makers from 123 countries and being involved in initial discussions on key issues makes it worth the effort to be a part of the meeting.
"There will be lots of hallway meetings, informal discussions, and U.S. agriculture wants to be a part of this," said an official with the American Farm Bureau Federation.
The Farm Bureau, the biggest producer group in the United States, will be represented in Singapore by three of its officials, including its president Dean Kleckner.
"This will be a stock-taking meeting where we assess how much we've accomplished in the first two years of WTO ... how much increased access we have, how much tarrifs have come down," said Rominger.
Although officials were cautious in their expectations, the agriculture contingent appears eager to address specific issues, depending on what sector the participants represent.
The almost 40 private sector officials represent a wide range of agricultural industries, including dairy, sugar, grains, fruits and vegetables, oilseeds and pork.
Dairy industry officials want to discuss a recent NAFTA panel ruling that upheld controversial Canadian duties on incoming shipments of U.S. dairy and poultry products.

Grain industry officials want to address the practice by some Latin American countries of requiring local industries to buy home-grown products before foreign-grown production. U.S. industry officials contend this is illegal under WTO.

Concerns that importing countries do not use new sanitary and phytosanitary issues as trade barriers will also be discussed. Recent trade disputes over regulations imposed because of alleged worries over animal and plant safety have prompted those discussions.
Rominger said, "In some cases in place of the old tarrifs that countries had, we see sanitary and phytosanitary barriers put up, and we think many of those are not based on sound science."
